summary: An 80-foot steel tower built by Tennessee in 1951 on Grassy Knob near Robbins, used for fire detection until 1967 and still maintained by the state.

facts.design: four-sided steel truss tower, 7x7 ft steel-framed cab

access.note: Maintained by TN Division of Forestry as an active fire-detection asset, not set up as a public rental; cab was locked at time of NRHP survey.

events.note: Built by the State of Tennessee; steel bears W.S. Co. manufacturer markings.
Used for fire detection from 1951 to 1967.
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register March 27, 2014.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places; exact listing year not confirmed by assembled sources (the NRHP registration form only states a 1951-1967 period of significance, and a 2017 'accessed' date in its bibliography was mistakenly read as the listing year in an earlier draft).

evidence.supports: built by State of Tennessee in 1951; still serviceable
evidence.quote: Also known locally as the Grassy Knob tower, Black Creek was built by the State of Tennessee in 1951. The tower is still serviceable when the need to use it arises.

evidence.supports: eighty-foot steel truss tower, galvanized steel, bolted connections, W.S. Co. markings
evidence.quote: The Black Creek Fire Lookout Tower (locally known as the Grassy Knob tower) is located in Scott County, in eastern Tennessee, and is an eighty-foot-tall skeletal steel structure
topped by an enclosed seven-foot by seven-foot square cab... Access to the observation room is achieved via a series of twelve steel staircases, each with eight wood plank treads.

evidence.supports: used 1951-1967, one of two towers still operated by TN Division of Forestry, outbuildings
evidence.quote: It is one of two fire towers in Scott County still maintained by the Tennessee Division of Forestry. It was used for fire detection from 1951 to 1967.

evidence.supports: operator's cabin now storage shed; crew house and other buildings
evidence.quote: Adjacent to the lookout tower is an operator's cabin, a crew house, and other buildings. All were constructed circa 1951... The operator's cabin is a 10 foot by 12 foot cabin originally used to provide shelter for fire spotter personnel. It is now used as a storage shed.

evidence.supports: NRHP listing recognizing engineering and conservation significance 1951-1967
evidence.quote: Areas Of Significance: ENGINEERING CONSERVATION Periods Of Significance: 1951 AD - 1967 AD

notes_for_editor: Current access level in the brief was 'unknown'; set to restricted based on NRHP note that the cab was locked during survey and the tower is an active state asset rather than a public rental. No conflicting build years found for this tower. Fact-check 2026-10-04: removed an unsupported '2017' NRHP-listing year (not stated by any cited source; the NRHP form's bibliography has a 2017 website-access date that appears to have been mistaken for the listing year) and corrected the footnote on the Clear Fork/New Rivers location detail, which is sourced to [3] (Encyclopedia of Scott County), not [1] (NHLR) alone.
